full_judgment:
9. In the present case, admittedly the deed of sale in question was duly executed by the defendants in suit. It is also found that the defendants are illiterate and, as such, they executed the deed in question by putting their LTI that is why it is imperative to consider that the executants had no knowledge about the quantum of land contained therein. The trial court in its judgment observed that in the present marker, selling of 13 decimals land at a consideration of Taka 3,000 only is not at all believable. Moreover, the plaintiffs could not produce any evidence to the effect that at the relevant time in the concerned area the property was sold at the rate shown in the sale deed in question. The appellate court in allowing the appeal shifted the burden of proof upon the defendants simply observing that the defendants did not deny the execution of the sale deed without considering other legal aspect of the proceedings. 

 12. The appellate court is in an error in supposing that in the present case no action under Registration Act could have been taken by the plaintiffs. It seems to have omitted to notice that documents can be presented for registration only by the executants but also by any person claiming under the document. Plaintiffs therefore, who had possession of the document, within time allowed for registration, could have presented it for registration and obtained summons for defendants' appearance under section 86 of the Registration Act. If defendants had appeared and admitted execution, the document would have been registered. If they had denied execution, registration would have been refused and the plaintiffs would have been entitled to get an enquiry before the registrar under sections 73-76 of the Registration Act. If defendants did not appear, the plaintiffs might have proved execution of the document and on such proof would have been entitled to registration. If the Registering Officer was not satisfied with their evidences of execution and refused to register, an appeal would have lain to the Registrar under section 72. If the decision of the Registrar under sections 72 or 76 had been adverse to the plaintiffs they would have had a remedy by suit under section 77 of the Registration Act. Plaintiffs had therefore, a complete remedy under the Act and not having chosen to follow it have only themselves to blame that the efficacy of the document has not been completed by registration.
